## Section 1: Has provincial reading changed since 2017?

```{r s1-data}
# School average share of students meeting the reading standard, by year.
# 2019 and 2020 stay NA (no tests) so the line breaks there.
trend <- elem |>
  group_by(start_year) |>
  summarise(`Grade 3` = mean(g3_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Grade 6` = mean(g6_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-start_year, names_to = "grade", values_to = "pct") |>
  complete(start_year = 2017:2024, grade)

trend |> filter(!is.na(pct)) |> pivot_wider(names_from = grade, values_from = pct)
```

```{r fig1, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.8}
ggplot(trend, aes(x = start_year, y = pct, colour = grade)) +
  # grey band for the two years without tests
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2018.55, xmax = 2020.45, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey93") +
  annotate("text", x = 2019.5, y = 64, label = "No provincial\ntests\n(COVID-19)",
           size = 3.2, colour = "grey40", lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  # label each line at its right end instead of using a legend
  geom_text(data = filter(trend, start_year == 2024),
            aes(label = paste0(grade, ": ", round(pct), "%")),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.15, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Grade 3" = "#333333", "Grade 6" = "#8C8C8C"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2017:2024, labels = year_label(2017:2024),
                     limits = c(2016.8, 2025.6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(60, 92), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Figure 1. The provincial average barely moves",
       subtitle = "Average share of students meeting the provincial reading standard",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story
```

Ontario's reading results have barely changed. In 2017-18, about 74% of Grade 3 students in the average school met the provincial reading standard, and in 2024-25 the figure was still about 74%, 0.1 percentage points lower. Grade 3 dipped after testing resumed in 2021-22 and reached about 71% in 2023-24, roughly 3 points below where it started, before recovering. Grade 6 results are higher and rose from 81% to 85% (Figure 1).

A parent looking at this chart might conclude that nothing has changed. An average can stay flat, though, while some schools improve and others fall behind. To check whether every school stayed the same, we split schools by how many of their students come from low-income households.

## Section 2: How big is the gap between the richest and poorest schools, and is it closing?

```{r s2-data}
# Average reading in the most affluent vs highest-poverty fifth of schools, by year
gap_df <- elem |>
  filter(income_group %in% c("Most affluent fifth", "Highest-poverty fifth")) |>
  group_by(start_year, income_group) |>
  summarise(`Grade 3` = mean(g3_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Grade 6` = mean(g6_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Grade 3`, `Grade 6`), names_to = "grade", values_to = "pct")

# One row per year and grade, with the gap in percentage points
gap_wide <- gap_df |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = income_group, values_from = pct) |>
  mutate(gap = `Most affluent fifth` - `Highest-poverty fifth`)

gap_wide |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !start_year, ~ round(.x, 1)))
```

```{r fig2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.4}
# Order years so the latest is at the top
gap_plot <- gap_df |>
  mutate(year_lab = factor(year_label(start_year),
                           levels = rev(year_label(sort(unique(start_year))))))
gap_seg <- gap_wide |>
  mutate(year_lab = factor(year_label(start_year), levels = levels(gap_plot$year_lab)))

ggplot() +
  # grey bar = the gap between the two groups
  geom_segment(data = gap_seg,
               aes(y = year_lab, yend = year_lab,
                   x = `Highest-poverty fifth`, xend = `Most affluent fifth`),
               colour = "grey80", linewidth = 2.2) +
  geom_point(data = gap_plot, aes(x = pct, y = year_lab, colour = income_group),
             size = 3.2) +
  # gap size written to the right of each row
  geom_text(data = gap_seg,
            aes(x = `Most affluent fifth` + 1.2, y = year_lab,
                label = paste0(round(gap), " pts")),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "grey25") +
  facet_wrap(~ grade) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = income_cols[c("Most affluent fifth", "Highest-poverty fifth")],
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(58, 97), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Figure 2. The Grade 3 gap is stuck; the Grade 6 gap is narrowing",
       subtitle = "Share of students meeting the reading standard:\nmost affluent vs highest-poverty fifth of schools",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
```

Once schools are split by income, the flat average hides a steady gap. In 2017-18, 80.5% of Grade 3 students in the most affluent fifth of schools met the reading standard, compared with 64.7% in the highest-poverty fifth, a gap of 15.8 percentage points. In 2024-25 the gap was 15.9 points, and in the years between it stayed between about 14.5 and 16 points (Figure 2). In a class of 30, that is roughly five more children in a high-poverty school who are not reading at the provincial standard.

Grade 6 has changed more. Before the pandemic the gap was about 15 points, the same as in Grade 3. When testing resumed in 2021-22 it had fallen to 11.5 points, and it stayed between about 10 and 13 points through 2024-25, ending at 10.1, about a third smaller than where it started.

The Grade 3 students of 2021-22 were the Grade 6 students of 2024-25. If the gap is fixed in Grade 3 but smaller in Grade 6, do the same children catch up as they get older?
